q2_0_3_0:
Role of Atropine in Organophosphate Poisoning

Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase → ↑ acetylcholine at muscarinic & nicotinic receptors → SLUDGE-BB (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI cramps, emesis, bradycardia, bronchospasm) + fasciculations, seizures, coma.

Atropine — competitive muscarinic antagonist; blocks excess ACh at muscarinic receptors → reverses bradycardia, bronchospasm, secretions, GI hypermotility. Does NOT reverse nicotinic effects (fasciculations, muscle weakness) — that requires pralidoxime (2-PAM).

Dose — 1.2–2 mg IV bolus; double every 5 min until "atropinisation" achieved (dry skin, HR >80, SBP >80, clear chest, pupils dilated); then infusion 10–20% of total loading dose per hour; titrate to maintain atropinisation for 24–48 h.

Clinical Pearl — Titrate to atropinisation (dry mouth, HR >80, clear chest); NOT to pupil size; continue infusion for days (lipid-soluble OP redistribution); always combine with pralidoxime (reverses nicotinic effects; reactivates AChE if given early — within 24–48 h).
q2_0_3_1:
Pharmacological Basis of Low-Dose Aspirin as Antiplatelet

Aspirin — irreversible acetylation of COX-1 in platelets → blocks thromboxane A2 (TXA2) synthesis → ↓ platelet aggregation for platelet lifespan (7–10 days).

Why low dose (75–150 mg)?

  • Platelets have no nucleus → cannot synthesise new COX-1 → irreversible inhibition lasts for platelet lifespan (7–10 days).
  • Endothelial cells (which produce prostacyclin — PGI2, antiplatelet) HAVE nucleus → can regenerate COX → recover within hours.
  • Low dose (75 mg) — selectively inhibits platelet COX-1 (TXA2) with minimal effect on endothelial COX-2 (PGI2) — preserves antithrombotic prostacyclin.
  • High dose (>300 mg) — inhibits both TXA2 & PGI2 — negates antithrombotic benefit.
  • Once daily dosing sufficient — new platelets produced daily (~10% turnover) but low dose maintains inhibition of TXA2.

Uses — secondary prevention (post-MI, stroke, PAD); primary prevention (controversial — ASCVD risk ≥7.5% per ACC/AHA; bleeding risk must be considered); pregnancy — anti-phospholipid syndrome.

Clinical Pearl — Low-dose aspirin (75 mg) selectively inhibits platelet TXA2 while sparing endothelial PGI2 (antithrombotic) — "selective antiplatelet effect". Higher doses may paradoxically reduce antithrombotic benefit by also inhibiting PGI2.
q2_0_3_2:
Pharmacological Basis of Theophylline in Asthma

Theophylline — methylxanthine bronchodilator; less commonly used now (narrow therapeutic index; replaced by ICS + LABA).

Mechanism:

  1. Phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibition — ↓ cAMP & cGMP breakdown → ↑ intracellular cAMP → ↓ intracellular Ca²⁺ → bronchial smooth muscle relaxation (bronchodilation).
  2. Adenosine receptor antagonism — adenosine causes bronchoconstriction in asthmatics; theophylline blocks A1 & A2 receptors → bronchodilation; also responsible for CNS stimulation & cardiac effects.
  3. Anti-inflammatory — ↑ histone deacetylase (HDAC) activity → ↓ inflammatory gene transcription; ↓ eosinophils & cytokines (similar to low-dose corticosteroid effect).
  4. ↑ Diaphragmatic contractility — improves respiratory muscle function.

Therapeutic range — 10–20 µg/mL; narrow therapeutic index; monitor levels; toxicity — arrhythmias, seizures (no warning; can be fatal), nausea, headache. Drug interactions — CYP1A2 & CYP3A4 metabolism; ↑ levels with erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, oral contraceptives; ↓ levels with rifampicin, phenytoin, smoking, barbiturates.

Clinical Pearl — Theophylline is now 3rd/4th-line for asthma (behind ICS, LABA, LTRA); used in severe persistent asthma or when ICS/LABA unavailable. Always monitor serum levels — 10–20 µg/mL; seizures can occur without warning at levels >25 µg/mL and are often fatal. Avoid in cardiac disease, seizure disorder, peptic ulcer.
q2_0_3_3:
Why Folinic Acid Preferred Over Folic Acid for Methotrexate Toxicity

Methotrexate — inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) → ↓ tetrahydrofolate (THF) → ↓ DNA synthesis (↓ thymidylate, ↓ purines) → stops rapidly dividing cells (cancer, psoriasis, RA).

Folic acid — must be reduced by DHFR to THF before it can function; if DHFR is inhibited by methotrexate, folic acid CANNOT be converted to active form → useless.

Folinic acid (leucovorin, 5-formyl-THF) — already reduced (bypasses DHFR); directly provides THF → restores DNA synthesis → rescues normal cells from methotrexate toxicity.

Uses:

  • Methotrexate rescue — after high-dose methotrexate (cancer); leucovorin given 24 h later to rescue normal cells.
  • Methotrexate overdose — accidental or intentional.
  • Trimethoprim/pyrimethamine toxicity — also DHFR inhibitors.
  • Colorectal cancer — 5-FU + leucovorin (enhances 5-FU binding to thymidylate synthase).

Clinical Pearl — Folinic acid (leucovorin) bypasses the blocked DHFR enzyme; folic acid requires DHFR (blocked by MTX) → useless. Never give leucovorin with methotrexate for cancer treatment — rescues tumour cells too! Only give after MTX has had time to act (rescue 24 h later).
q2_0_3_4:
Why Loading Doses Required for Drugs Like Digoxin

Loading dose — initial higher dose to rapidly achieve therapeutic plasma concentration; needed when:

  1. Long half-life — drug takes too long to reach steady state by regular dosing alone (digoxin t½ 36 h; takes 5 half-lives = 7 days to reach steady state); loading achieves therapeutic level in hours.
  2. Large volume of distribution (Vd) — drug distributes widely in tissues (digoxin Vd ~500 L; binds to Na-K-ATPase in muscle); large loading dose needed to saturate tissue binding & achieve therapeutic plasma level.
  3. Urgent therapeutic need — e.g., digoxin for acute AF rate control; phenytoin for status epilepticus; amiodarone for VT.

Formula — Loading dose = (Vd × Target plasma concentration) / Bioavailability

For digoxin — Vd 7 L/kg; target 1.5 ng/mL; loading dose = 7 × 1.5 × 70 kg = 735 µg (give as 0.5 mg + 0.25 mg × 2 at 6 h intervals).

Other drugs needing loading — amiodarone (Vd 60 L/kg; t½ 50 days), phenytoin (status epilepticus), procainamide, digoxin, voriconazole, chloroquine.

Clinical Pearl — Loading dose is needed when drug has long half-life & urgent effect needed; without loading, takes 5 half-lives (3.3 × t½) to reach 90% steady state — too slow for digoxin (7 days), amiodarone (250 days!).
q2_0_3_5:
Methods for Prolongation of Drug Action

  1. Sustained/Extended release formulations — matrix tablets, coated beads, osmotic pumps (e.g., nifedipine GITS, metoprolol succinate ER); slow release over 12–24 h; once-daily dosing.
  2. Transdermal patches — nitroglycerin, fentanyl, oestrogen, clonidine, rivastigmine, rotigotine; sustained release through skin over 24–72 h.
  3. Depot injections — IM/SC; oily vehicle or microspheres; haloperidol decanoate, fluphenazine decanoate, medroxyprogesterone acetate (Depo-Provera), risperidone microspheres, paliperidone palmitate, olanzapine pamoate; weekly to monthly dosing.
  4. Prodrugs — inactive form converted to active in body slowly; enalapril → enalaprilat; valacyclovir → acyclovir; tenofovir disoproxil → tenofovir.
  5. Chemical modification — add bulky group; esterification (benzathine penicillin — IM; duration 3–4 weeks); procaine penicillin (12–24 h).
  6. Bioerodible implants — subcutaneous; sustained release; contraceptive implants (etonogestrel — 3 years; levonorgestrel — 5 years).
  7. Liposomal formulations — liposomal amphotericin B, liposomal doxorubicin; sustained release; reduced toxicity.
  8. Pegylation — attach PEG (polyethylene glycol); pegylated interferon (t½ 80 h vs 8 h standard); pegfilgrastim (once per cycle vs daily filgrastim); pegvisomant.
  9. Protein binding — highly protein-bound drugs have longer duration (warfarin 99% bound).
  10. Active metabolites — diazepam → nordiazepam (t½ 100 h); extended duration.

Clinical Pearl — Prolongation of drug action improves adherence (less frequent dosing), reduces side effects (smoother plasma levels), and enables outpatient treatment of chronic diseases (antipsychotic depots, contraceptive implants, transdermal patches).
q2_0_3_6:
Mucolytics

Mucolytics — drugs that break down or reduce viscosity of mucus; used for productive cough with thick secretions (COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis).

Classification

  1. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) — breaks disulphide bonds in mucus glycoproteins → ↓ viscosity; direct; also antioxidant (↑ glutathione); used in COPD, CF, paracetamol overdose (antidote — restores glutathione).
  2. Carbocisteine — breaks disulphide bonds; also ↓ mucus secretion; oral; for COPD, chronic bronchitis.
  3. Erdosteine — prodrug; breaks disulphide bonds; also antibacterial (↑ ciliary function); for acute exacerbation of COPD.
  4. Bromhexine — breaks mucus polymers; also ↑ ciliary activity; metabolised to ambroxol.
  5. Ambroxol — active metabolite of bromhexine; ↑ surfactant production; ↓ mucus viscosity; anaesthetic effect (lozenge for sore throat).
  6. Dornase alfa (recombinant human DNase) — breaks down DNA in pus (from neutrophils) → ↓ viscosity; inhaled; for cystic fibrosis; NOT for COPD.
  7. Hypertonic saline (7%) — osmotic; draws water into mucus → ↓ viscosity; inhaled; for CF; also for bronchiectasis.

Uses

  • COPD exacerbation — carbocisteine, erdosteine, NAC.
  • Cystic fibrosis — dornase alfa, hypertonic saline, NAC.
  • Bronchiectasis — NAC, hypertonic saline.
  • Paracetamol overdose — IV NAC (antidote; restores hepatic glutathione).

Clinical Pearl — N-acetylcysteine is the most versatile mucolytic — breaks mucus disulphide bonds AND is antidote for paracetamol overdose (restores glutathione). Dornase alfa (rhDNase) — specific for cystic fibrosis (breaks DNA in purulent sputum); NOT effective in COPD (mucus is DNA-poor). Steam inhalation & oral hydration — cheapest & safest mucolytics; ↑ water content of mucus → ↓ viscosity.
q2_0_3_7:
Pharmacological Basis of Prazosin in BPH

Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) — enlarged prostate → compression of urethra → urinary symptoms (frequency, urgency, hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete emptying, nocturia).

Prazosin — selective α1-adrenergic receptor antagonist; blocks α1 receptors on:

  1. Prostate capsule, bladder neck, & urethral smooth muscle (α1A predominant) → relaxation → ↓ dynamic component of obstruction → improved urine flow, reduced symptoms.
  2. Peripheral vascular smooth muscle (α1B) → vasodilation → ↓ blood pressure (may be beneficial if coexisting hypertension; may cause postural hypotension).

Rationale: Prostatic & bladder neck smooth muscle tone is mediated by sympathetic α1-adrenergic receptors; blocking these receptors relaxes the prostate & bladder neck → relieves the "dynamic" component of BPH obstruction (as opposed to the "static" component — enlarged gland tissue, addressed by 5α-reductase inhibitors like finasteride).

Other α1-blockers for BPH — tamsulosin (uroselective — α1A; less hypotension; preferred), silodosin (α1A highly selective), doxazosin, terazosin, alfuzosin.

Clinical Pearl — Tamsulosin (uroselective α1A) is preferred for BPH — less postural hypotension than prazosin/doxazosin (less α1B effect on vascular smooth muscle). α1-blockers address the dynamic component (muscle tone); 5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) address the static component (gland size); combination for severe BPH. First-dose hypotension "first-dose effect" — start low (prazosin 0.5 mg), give at bedtime; especially in elderly. IFIS (Intraoperative Floppy Iris Syndrome) — tamsulosin causes iris instability during cataract surgery; inform ophthalmologist.
q2_0_3_8:
Pharmacological Basis of Adrenaline in Anaphylactic Shock

Anaphylaxis — Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity → massive mast cell & basophil degranulation → histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, PAF → vasodilation (↓ BP, shock), bronchospasm, ↑ vascular permeability (oedema, laryngeal obstruction), urticaria, GI cramps.

Adrenaline (epinephrine) — physiological antagonist of histamine (acts at DIFFERENT receptors to produce OPPOSITE effects):

  • α1 (vasoconstriction) — reverses vasodilation & hypotension; ↓ mucosal oedema (laryngeal, bronchial) → relieves upper airway obstruction.
  • β1 (cardiac) — ↑ heart rate, contractility → ↑ cardiac output → ↑ BP; counteracts bradycardia.
  • β2 (bronchodilation) — relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → reverses bronchospasm; ↓ mast cell mediator release (stabilises mast cells); ↑ cAMP in mast cells → ↓ degranulation.
  • β2 (metabolic) — ↑ glucose; ↓ allergy mediator release.

Why adrenaline (not other drugs)? — Only adrenaline acts on ALL relevant receptors (α1 + β1 + β2) simultaneously; antihistamines only block H1 (slow onset; incomplete); corticosteroids take hours to act; β2-agonists only bronchodilate (no vascular effect). Adrenaline is "all-in-one" — vasoconstrictor + bronchodilator + mast cell stabiliser + cardiac stimulant.

Dose — 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) IM into anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5 min if no response; IV 50–100 µg (1 mL of 1:10,000) if cardiac arrest or profound shock.

Clinical Pearl — Adrenaline is the ONLY life-saving drug in anaphylaxis — give IM 0.5 mg into anterolateral thigh ASAP; do NOT delay for IV access; repeat every 5 min; antihistamines, steroids, fluids, oxygen are adjuncts — NOT substitutes for adrenaline. Always prescribe EpiPen (epinephrine autoinjector) for patients with history of anaphylaxis. IV adrenaline only if cardiac arrest or profound shock — risk of arrhythmia if given too rapidly.
q2_0_3_9:
Drug for Reversal of Competitive Neuromuscular Blockade

Neostigmine — acetylcholinesterase inhibitor — is the drug of choice for reversal of competitive (non-depolarising) neuromuscular blockade (e.g., vecuronium, rocuronium, atracurium).

Mechanism:

  1. Inhibits acetylcholinesterase → ↑ acetylcholine at NMJ.
  2. Excess ACh competes with non-depolarising NMBA for nicotinic (N2) receptors → displaces NMBA → restores neuromuscular transmission.

Co-administered with atropine or glycopyrrolate — neostigmine also increases ACh at muscarinic receptors → bradycardia, bronchospasm, salivation, GI hypermotility; anticholinergic prevents these.

Dose — neostigmine 0.04–0.07 mg/kg IV + glycopyrrolate 0.01 mg/kg IV (or atropine 0.02 mg/kg).

Limitations:

  • Cannot reverse deep block effectively (TOF count 0–1) — wait for spontaneous recovery first.
  • Cannot reverse depolarising block (succinylcholine) — actually prolongs it.
  • Side effects — bradycardia (without atropine), nausea, bronchospasm.

Newer alternative — Sugammadex — modified γ-cyclodextrin; encapsulates rocuronium/vecuronium (forms inactive complex) → direct removal; does NOT require AChE inhibition; no muscarinic side effects; can reverse deep block immediately; dose 2–4 mg/kg IV; expensive.

Clinical Pearl — Neostigmine + glycopyrrolate is standard reversal; sugammadex is revolutionary — encapsulates rocuronium directly; reverses even deep block immediately; no muscarinic side effects; expensive but game-changer for "cannot intubate, cannot ventilate" situations (rocuronium → immediate reversal with sugammadex 16 mg/kg). Always confirm adequate reversal — train-of-four (TOF) ratio ≥0.9; clinical criteria — sustained head lift >5 sec, grip strength, vital capacity.
q2_0_3_10:
Drug Therapy of Acute Congestive Glaucoma (Angle-Closure)

Acute angle-closure glaucoma — sudden closure of iridocorneal angle → blocked aqueous outflow → rapidly ↑ IOP (50–80 mmHg) → severe eye pain, headache, blurred vision, halos, nausea/vomiting, fixed mid-dilated pupil, corneal oedema. Ophthalmic emergency — vision loss within hours.

Immediate Medical Therapy

  1. Topical β-blocker — Timolol 0.5%, 1 drop; ↓ aqueous humour production.
  2. Topical α2-agonist — Brimonidine 0.15%, 1 drop; ↓ aqueous production & ↑ uveoscleral outflow.
  3. Systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor — Acetazolamide 500 mg IV or PO; ↓ aqueous humour production; most effective systemic agent.
  4. Topical steroid — Prednisolone acetate 1%, 1 drop QID; ↓ inflammation.
  5. Hyperosmotic agent — Mannitol 20% 1–2 g/kg IV over 45 min OR glycerol 1–1.5 g/kg PO; draws fluid from eye → ↓ IOP; for very high IOP.
  6. Analgesia & antiemetic — for comfort.
  7. Pilocarpine 1–2% — miotic; constricts pupil → opens angle; NOT effective while IOP >40 mmHg (iris sphincter ischaemic); give AFTER IOP reduced (e.g., after 1 h of above therapy).

Definitive Treatment

  • Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) — creates hole in peripheral iris → bypasses pupillary block → equalises pressure between posterior & anterior chambers → opens angle; definitive; performed after IOP controlled & cornea clears (24–48 h).
  • Surgical iridectomy — if laser not possible.
  • Prophylactic LPI in fellow eye — prevent attack (50% risk in 5 years).

Clinical Pearl — Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency — reduce IOP within hours to prevent permanent optic nerve damage. Immediate: timolol + brimonidine + acetazolamide IV + mannitol if severe; pilocarpine AFTER IOP <40 (ischaemic sphincter won't respond). Definitive: laser peripheral iridotomy (creates alternative aqueous outflow pathway). Always treat fellow eye prophylactically — narrow angles are bilateral; 50% risk of attack in fellow eye within 5 years. Avoid mydriatics/anticholinergics in patients with narrow angles — precipitate attack.
q2_0_3_11:
Effects of Atropine on Eyes & Uses/Contraindications

Effects on Eye

  • Mydriasis (pupil dilation) — blocks M3 on iris sphincter → unopposed α1 (dilator) → dilation.
  • Cycloplegia (paralysis of accommodation) — blocks M3 on ciliary muscle → cannot contract for near vision → blurred near vision.
  • ↑ Intraocular pressure — in angle-closure glaucoma (dilated iris blocks trabecular meshwork → ↑ IOP); no effect or minimal in open-angle.
  • Photophobia — due to mydriasis.

Therapeutic Uses (Ophthalmological)

  • Refraction testing in children — cycloplegic refraction (atropine 1%, homatropine 2%, cyclopentolate 1%); paralyse accommodation for accurate measurement.
  • Treatment of uveitis/iritis — cycloplegia prevents synechiae (adhesions between iris & lens); rests ciliary muscle (relieves pain).
  • Amblyopia (lazy eye) — atropine 1% in good eye → forces child to use amblyopic eye ("penalisation").
  • Mydriasis for fundoscopy — tropicamide (short-acting; preferred), phenylephrine (α1; no cycloplegia).

Systemic Uses (Related)

  • Organophosphorus poisoning antidote (muscarinic antagonist).
  • Pre-anaesthetic medication (↓ secretions, ↓ vagal reflexes).
  • Bradycardia, AV block (↑ HR).
  • Antispasmodic (GI, biliary, renal colic).

Contraindications for Ophthalmic Use

  • Angle-closure glaucoma — mydriasis precipitates acute attack; ↑ IOP.
  • Known hypersensitivity.
  • Children with Down syndrome, cerebral palsy — ↑ sensitivity (paradoxical reaction; hyperthermia).
  • Elderly with BPH — urinary retention (systemic absorption).
  • Tachycardia — systemic absorption → ↑ HR.

Clinical Pearl — Atropine is longest-acting mydriatic/cycloplegic (7–14 days); tropicamide is preferred for fundoscopy (short duration — 3–6 h; no cycloplegia); cyclopentolate for refraction in children (onset 30 min; duration 24 h); atropine for uveitis & amblyopia (long-acting; preferred for sustained cycloplegia). NEVER use atropine/mydriatics in angle-closure glaucoma — dilated iris blocks trabecular meshwork → acute attack → blindness.
q2_0_3_12:
Why Cisatracurium Preferred for Liver/Kidney Disease

Cisatracurium — non-depolarising neuromuscular blocker (benzylisoquinolinium); stereoisomer of atracurium.

Organ-independent elimination — Hofmann elimination:

  • Cisatracurium is degraded by Hofmann elimination — spontaneous non-enzymatic degradation at physiological pH & temperature → cleaved into laudanosine & monoquaternary acrylate.
  • Does NOT require liver, kidney, or plasma cholinesterase for elimination.
  • Independent of organ function → safe in hepatic & renal failure.
  • Also some non-specific ester hydrolysis (independent of plasma cholinesterase).

Advantages in liver/kidney disease:

  • No accumulation in renal failure (unlike vecuronium, rocuronium — hepatic/renal excretion).
  • No accumulation in hepatic failure (unlike vecuronium, rocuronium — hepatic metabolism).
  • Predictable recovery regardless of organ function.
  • No histamine release (unlike atracurium — less hypotension, bronchospasm).
  • Less laudanosine than atracurium (laudanosine — CNS excitation, seizures in high doses; less concern with cisatracurium).

Comparison with other NMBAs in organ failure:

  • Vacuronium — hepatic metabolism + renal excretion → accumulates in both liver & kidney disease.
  • Rocuronium — hepatic excretion → accumulates in liver disease; sugammadex reversal is renal-cleared (problematic in CKD).
  • Atracurium — Hofmann elimination (organ-independent) but histamine release → hypotension, bronchospasm.
  • Cisatracurium — Hofmann elimination + no histamine release → safest for organ failure & haemodynamically unstable patients.

Clinical Pearl — Cisatracurium is the NMBA of choice for ICU patients with hepatic or renal failure — Hofmann elimination (pH & temperature-dependent non-enzymatic degradation) makes it organ-independent; no accumulation; no histamine release (unlike atracurium). Also preferred in haemodynamically unstable patients — no cardiovascular effects. ICU sedation/paralysis — cisatracurium infusion for ARDS, severe asthma, elevated ICP. Laudanosine (metabolite) — CNS excitation; theoretical seizure risk with very high doses or prolonged infusion; less than atracurium.
q2_0_3_13:
Why Sacubitril/Valsartan Preferred Over ACEI in Chronic Heart Failure

Sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto) — ARNI (Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibitor) — combination of:

  • Valsartan — ARB; blocks AT1 receptor → ↓ angiotensin II effects (vasoconstriction, aldosterone, remodelling).
  • Sacubitril — prodrug; converted to sacubitrilat (active); inhibits neprilysin — enzyme that degrades natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP, CNP) → ↑ natriuretic peptides → vasodilation, natriuresis, diuresis, ↓ fibrosis, ↓ remodelling.

Why preferred over ACE inhibitor?

  1. PARI GMENT-HF trial (2014) — sacubitril/valsartan reduced CV mortality & HF hospitalisation by 20% vs enalapril in HFrEF; stopped early due to benefit.
  2. Dual mechanism — blocks RAAS (valsartan) AND enhances natriuretic peptide system (sacubitril) → more comprehensive neurohormonal modulation than ACEI alone.
  3. ↑ Natriuretic peptides → vasodilation, natriuresis, ↓ fibrosis, ↓ hypertrophy — additional benefit beyond RAAS blockade.
  4. Less cough & angioedema than ACEI — ARB (not ACEI) → no bradykinin potentiation (less cough, angioedema).
  5. Superior outcomes — reduced all-cause mortality, CV mortality, HF hospitalisation; improved symptoms & quality of life.

Indications:

  • HFrEF (EF ≤40%) — NYHA II–IV; replaces ACEI/ARB as first-line (ESC 2016 guidelines).
  • Post-MI with LV dysfunction (PARADISE-MI trial — emerging).

Cautions:

  • Do NOT combine with ACEI (↑ angioedema risk) — washout 36 h after stopping ACEI before starting ARNI.
  • Do NOT use in pregnancy (teratogenic — ARB component).
  • Do NOT use in hereditary angioedema.
  • Caution in severe renal impairment, hyperkalaemia.

Clinical Pearl — PARADIGM-HF trial showed sacubitril/valsartan reduced mortality 20% vs enalapril — first drug in decades to show superiority over ACEI in HFrEF. Replace ACEI/ARB with ARNI in symptomatic HFrEF (NYHA II–IV, EF ≤40%). 36-hour washout from ACEI before starting ARNI (risk of angioedema if combined). Monitor K⁺, renal function — may cause hyperkalaemia & AKI (like ACEI/ARB). Start low (24/26 mg or 49/51 mg BD), titrate to target (97/103 mg BD).
q2_0_3_14:
Why Thiazides Preferred Over Loop Diuretics in Recurrent Calcium Stones

Idiopathic hypercalciuria — most common metabolic abnormality in calcium stone formers; ↑ urinary calcium → calcium oxalate/phosphate stone formation.

Thiazide diuretics — reduce urinary calcium excretion (paradoxical effect):

  1. Block Na-Cl cotransporter in DCT → ↓ intracellular Na → ↑ Na-Ca exchange on basolateral membrane → ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption (paracellular) → ↓ urinary Ca²⁺.
  2. ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption in DCT → ↓ urinary calcium → ↓ calcium oxalate supersaturation → ↓ stone formation.

Loop diuretics — INCREASE urinary calcium (opposite effect):

  • Block NKCC2 in TAL → ↓ positive lumen potential → ↓ paracellular Ca²⁺ & Mg²⁺ reabsorption → ↑ urinary Ca²⁺ → ↑ stone risk.
  • Used for hypercalcaemia (with IV saline) — opposite of thiazide.

Therefore — thiazides are preferred (↓ urinary Ca²⁺ → ↓ stones); loop diuretics are contraindicated (↑ urinary Ca²⁺ → ↑ stones).

Clinical use:

  • Hydrochlorothiazide 25–50 mg/day OR chlorthalidone 25 mg/day OR indapamide 2.5 mg/day.
  • Indicated for recurrent calcium stones with hypercalciuria.
  • Also ↓ new stone formation in normocalciuric stone formers.
  • Monitor K⁺ (hypokalaemia → ↓ citrate excretion → ↑ stone risk; supplement K⁺ or use K-sparing diuretic).
  • Monitor Na⁺ (↓ Na intake → ↓ urinary Ca²⁺).

Clinical Pearl — Thiazides reduce urinary calcium (↑ reabsorption in DCT) → reduce calcium stone formation; loop diuretics increase urinary calcium → promote stones. Always check 24-hour urinary calcium in recurrent stone formers; thiazide indicated if hypercalciuria (>4 mg/kg/day in men, >3.5 in women). Combine with K⁺ supplementation or amiloride — hypokalaemia ↓ citrate excretion → ↑ stone risk (citrate is stone inhibitor). Also advise ↑ fluid intake (>2 L/day), ↓ dietary sodium, normal dietary calcium, ↓ animal protein, ↓ oxalate foods.
q2_0_3_15:
Phenoxybenzamine in Pheochromocytoma Surgery

Phenoxybenzamine — irreversible alpha-blocker (alpha1+alpha2); given pre-operatively (7-14 days) and intra-operatively during pheochromocytoma surgery. Rationale: (1) Blocks alpha1 receptors → vasodilation → controls BP, expands contracted blood volume; (2) Must give alpha-blocker BEFORE beta-blocker — if beta-blocker first, unopposed alpha → hypertensive crisis; (3) Irreversible blockade preferred over competitive (phentolamine) — cannot be overcome by massive catecholamine release during tumour manipulation; (4) Intra-operative: prevents hypertensive crisis during tumour handling; after tumour removal, sudden catecholamine drop → hypotension (prepare with fluids, vasopressors). Clinical Pearl: Start phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BD, titrate to 20-40 mg TID/QID, 7-14 days pre-op; add beta-blocker only after alpha-blockade established (day 3-4); goal: BP <140/90 seated with orthostatic drop but SBP >90; expand volume with IV saline.
q2_0_3_16:
Neostigmine Preferred Over Physostigmine in Myasthenia Gravis

Neostigmine preferred because: (1) Quaternary ammonium compound — does NOT cross BBB (charged molecule) → no CNS side effects; acts selectively at peripheral NMJ; (2) Physostigmine — tertiary amine; crosses BBB → CNS effects (confusion, seizures, bradycardia, excessive salivation, bronchoconstriction); (3) Neostigmine — more selective for NMJ; available oral (15-30 mg TID) and IM/IV; (4) Pyridostigmine (Mestinon) actually preferred over neostigmine for chronic MG (longer duration, less muscarinic side effects; 60 mg TID-QID). Clinical Pearl: Pyridostigmine is drug of choice for MG; neostigmine IV for myasthenic crisis; physostigmine is NOT used for MG (crosses BBB — CNS toxicity); physostigmine is used for anticholinergic poisoning (reverses CNS anticholinergic effects).
q2_0_3_17:
Why Folic Acid Added When Treating B12 Deficiency

B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia by impairing folate utilization ("folate trap" — B12 is cofactor for methionine synthase which regenerates THF from N5-methyl-THF). When B12 is given, folate utilization resumes → folate stores may be depleted → concurrent folic acid prevents folate deficiency. Some patients have combined B12 + folate deficiency. CRITICAL CAUTION: Never give folic acid ALONE in B12 deficiency — folic acid will correct anaemia (bypasses folate trap) but will NOT prevent/reverse neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive decline). Only B12 prevents neurological complications. Always give B12 first (or simultaneously). Clinical Pearl: Always check B12 before treating megaloblastic anaemia with folic acid; folic acid alone corrects anaemia but allows irreversible neurological damage to progress. Treat with B12 IM hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg on alternate days × 2 weeks; add folic acid 5 mg/day only if folate deficiency confirmed.
q2_0_3_18:
Adrenaline as Physiological Antagonist to Histamine in Anaphylaxis

Adrenaline is a PHYSIOLOGICAL antagonist — acts at DIFFERENT receptors (adrenoceptors, NOT histamine receptors) to produce OPPOSITE effects: alpha1 → vasoconstriction (reverses histamine vasodilation → ↑ BP, ↓ oedema); beta1 → ↑ cardiac output (reverses hypotension); beta2 → bronchodilation (reverses bronchospasm) + ↓ mast cell degranulation (↑ cAMP). Why not antihistamines? — H1 antihistamines are SLOW (30-60 min), don't block H2 effects, don't reverse bronchospasm/hypotension effectively. Why not steroids? — take 4-6 h to act; useful for preventing biphasic reaction but NOT acute. Clinical Pearl: Adrenaline is the ONLY drug that reverses ALL manifestations of anaphylaxis simultaneously; IM 0.5 mg into anterolateral thigh ASAP; repeat every 5 min; antihistamines & steroids are ADJUNCTS, not substitutes.
q2_0_3_19:
Why Dantrolene Used in Malignant Hyperthermia

Malignant hyperthermia (MH) — RYR1 mutation; triggered by volatile anaesthetics & succinylcholine → uncontrolled Ca2+ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum → sustained muscle contraction → hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, acidosis. Dantrolene — blocks ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on sarcoplasmic reticulum → ↓ Ca2+ release → muscle relaxation. Only drug that directly blocks the pathophysiological mechanism; all other muscle relaxants act at NMJ or CNS — ineffective. Dose: 2.5 mg/kg IV rapid bolus; repeat every 5 min (max 10 mg/kg). Also used for NMS, severe serotonin syndrome. Clinical Pearl: Dantrolene is the ONLY specific antidote for MH; give IV 2.5 mg/kg immediately when MH suspected (↑ ETCO2, tachycardia, rigidity, hyperthermia after anaesthesia); also stop triggering agent, hyperventilate with 100% O2, cool patient, treat hyperkalaemia/acidosis. MH cart should be available in every OT.
q2_0_3_20:
Why Alpha Blocker Before Beta Blocker in Pheochromocytoma

If beta-blocker given FIRST without alpha-blockade: beta2 blockade removes vasodilatory effect of adrenaline on skeletal muscle blood vessels → alpha1-mediated vasoconstriction is UNOPPOSED → massive vasoconstriction → hypertensive crisis, stroke, MI, death. If alpha-blocker given FIRST: alpha1 blockade → vasodilation → controls hypertension; then beta-blocker can be added to control tachycardia. Sequence: alpha-blocker (phenoxybenzamine 7-14 days pre-op) → beta-blocker (propranolol day 3-4 after alpha-blockade). Clinical Pearl: ALWAYS alpha before beta in pheochromocytoma; beta-blocker alone → unopposed alpha → hypertensive crisis.

Why Novel Drug Delivery Systems Preferred Over Conventional

Advantages: (1) Controlled/sustained release → maintains therapeutic levels, avoids peaks/troughs, ↓ side effects, ↓ dosing frequency, ↑ adherence; (2) Targeted delivery → ↑ efficacy, ↓ systemic toxicity (liposomal doxorubicin — less cardiotoxicity; antibody-drug conjugates); (3) Improved bioavailability — protects from degradation; (4) Reduced dosing frequency — once daily to yearly (depot antipsychotics, contraceptive implants, zoledronic acid yearly); (5) Patient compliance — better adherence; (6) Reduced side effects — lower peak levels; (7) Protection of drug from acid, first-pass metabolism, enzymatic degradation; (8) Site-specific delivery — colon (IBD), brain (BBB bypass), intracellular (gene therapy, mRNA vaccines). Examples: transdermal patches, liposomes, nanoparticles, implants, PEGylated proteins, mRNA COVID vaccines. Clinical Pearl: NDDS transform pharmacotherapy — sustained release (adherence), targeted delivery (less toxicity), protection (bioavailability). mRNA COVID vaccines (lipid nanoparticles) demonstrated NDDS at population scale.

Why Selective Beta Blockers Preferred Over Non-Selective

Selective beta1-blockers preferred because: (1) Bronchospasm — non-selective block beta2 → bronchospasm in asthma/COPD; selective beta1 spare beta2 → safer; (2) Metabolic — non-selective mask hypoglycaemia symptoms & impair recovery; selective less effect; safer in diabetics; (3) Peripheral vascular — non-selective block beta2 vasodilation → cold extremities, Raynaud's, claudication; selective less effect; (4) Lipid profile — non-selective ↑ triglycerides, ↓ HDL more; selective less; carvedilol/nebivolol neutral; (5) Exercise tolerance — non-selective reduce more. Selectivity is dose-dependent — lost at high doses. Clinical Pearl: Beta1-selective (atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) preferred in HTN with asthma/COPD, diabetes, PAD, elderly. Nebivolol — most selective + NO-mediated vasodilation. Carvedilol (alpha1+beta) — preferred in diabetes & HF.
